rashi:a1.1: To be shorn and to be worked: [they do not go out to non-sacred status with permission to be shorn and worked,] but only like the law of sacrificial animals whose consecration preceded their blemish, which, when they are redeemed, have no permission for shearing and labor but only permission to be eaten, as we say in the second chapter of Bekhorot (14a). This is not so with sacrificial animals whose blemish preceded their consecration, which go out to non-sacred status through redemption, to be shorn and to be worked, as we say there in Bekhorot. But with regard to substitution the verse revealed (Leviticus 27:10) “a good for a bad, or a bad for a good”: it did not distinguish between an unblemished animal and a blemished one.
rashi:a4.1: GEMARA. With regard to a substitute he is flogged: for the verse included in it unwitting like intentional.
rashi:a4.2: With regard to sacrificial animals he is not flogged: for we do not find lashes except for one who acts intentionally and with forewarning.
rashi:a7.1: He thought to say: The black ox that comes out of my house first shall be a substitute in place of this one, and there came out of his mouth “white ox.” With regard to substitution it is consecrated and he is flogged, for the verse revealed it.
rashi:a7.2: With regard to sacrificial animals: if it is a blemished animal [consecrated] for the altar, he is not flogged, since it is not consecrated at all, for consecration in error is not consecration.
rashi:a8.1: Let this one go out and let that one enter: and that consecrated animal is unblemished and does not go out to non-sacred status; rather, this one is caught up in its sanctity and becomes a substitute. He thought that it would go out to non-sacred status like a blemished animal, and he did not intend to substitute, and even so he is flogged. And with regard to sacrificial animals, too, it is a case similar to this: he knew that sacrificial animals are forbidden to non-priests, but he thought that where a blemish befell them they are eaten without redemption. That is similar to this one, who knew that substitution is forbidden but thought that in such a manner it is permitted.
rashi:a9.1: And he entered and consecrated and substituted without his awareness: for he is a man lost in his thoughts and did not know what he was saying. With regard to substitution it is consecrated and he is flogged, for the verse revealed unwitting like intentional.
rashi:a9.2: With regard to sacrificial animals: it is not consecrated, and if it is a blemished animal [consecrated] for the altar, he is not flogged, since it is not consecrated, for it is consecration in error.
rashi:a10.1: They are not sanctified through substitution: even though with substitution inherent sanctity takes effect on an animal with a permanent blemish, it does not take effect on these. All the more so, inherent sanctity does not take effect on them through consecration by speech, but only sanctity of value, like wood and stones, and they do not require a blemish to be redeemed.
rashi:a10.2: And they do not sanctify: others through substitution, if they are consecrated.
rashi:a11.1: And Rabbi Meir explains how they can be consecrated, such that it needs to be said that they do not sanctify.
rashi:a11.2: In one who consecrates an animal: on which sanctity takes effect.
rashi:a11.3: And afterward it became a tereifa: (even though it is consecrated). In this case it was necessary to say that even though it is consecrated, it does not effect substitution. But diverse kinds, a tumtum and a hermaphrodite were spoiled from the outset of their creation and do not have that sanctity.
rashi:a11.4: Only in the offspring of sacrificial animals: whose mother was consecrated before she became pregnant, for then they are consecrated of themselves, since a fetus is like the thigh of its mother. And in this case it was necessary to say that they do not effect substitution.
rashi:a11.5: And according to Rabbi Yehuda, who said: that with other offspring of sacrificial animals the offspring effects substitution, it was necessary to teach us about these that they do not effect substitution and that inherent sanctity does not take effect on them even through substitution. And the ones we mentioned are not “bad from the outset” [i.e., blemished before they were consecrated], for we established it as one who consecrates an animal and afterward it became a tereifa, one who consecrates a fetus, etc.; and the tumtum and the hermaphrodite are consecrated by virtue of their mother before they were formed.
rashi:a13.1: But there is a blemished animal, which is not sacrificed, and inherent sanctity takes effect on it: through substitution, as the mishna teaches that substitution takes effect, etc. And if its consecration preceded its blemish, it effects substitution, as it is written: “a good for a bad.” So this animal too, whose consecration preceded its becoming a tereifa, should effect substitution; and if it became a tereifa while it was non-sacred, it should be caught up [in sanctity] through substitution.
rashi:a13.2: Is sacrificed in its kind: other, unblemished animals. But all these five are not sacrificed in their kind. An animal born by caesarean section is not considered of the kind of other animals, for people would be astonished at it.
rashi:a14.1: An inherent disqualification: and all of these are inherent disqualifications without anything lacking, such as a perforated membrane of the brain or a perforated abomasum. But a blemish is merely a disqualification of something lacking.
rashi:a15.1: But isn’t “too long” and “closed” written in the passage (Leviticus 22:23) about blemished animals: and these are inherent disqualifications without anything lacking, and even so they effect substitution, as it is written: “a good for a bad.” So my teacher explained.
rashi:a17.1: What did you say, that a tereifa also has its kind? It is not similar to a blemished animal, for a non-kosher animal is forbidden for consumption and a tereifa is forbidden for consumption, to exclude a blemished animal, which is permitted for consumption: that is to say, even if a tereifa is not compared to a non-kosher animal in this matter, since its kind is sacrificed, it is compared to it in another matter, that it is forbidden for consumption like it.
rashi:a18.1: It requires a permanent blemish, etc.: for Shmuel holds that inherent sanctity takes effect on it.
rashi:a18.2: Conclude from it, etc.: but we hold (below, Temurah 31a) that one does not redeem sacrificial animals to feed them to dogs; rather, [they are left] to die.
rashi:a19.1: Like one who consecrates wood [Rashi’s heading adds, in parentheses, “and sulfur,” where the daf reads “and stones”]: and they are redeemed to be fed to dogs, for they are not called sacrificial animals.
rashi:a21.1: This is how we read: “They raised an objection: Rabbi Eliezer [the daf reads Rabbi Elazar] says, etc.” This we read first, and afterward that one: “All sacrificial animals that became tereifa.”
tosafot:a4.1: With regard to substitution he is flogged; with regard to sacrificial animals he is not flogged: And some books read: “With regard to substitution it is consecrated,” etc. According to the first reading, the reason one who substitutes unwittingly is flogged is that it is a decree of the verse, since “shall be” is written, to include unwitting like intentional. Rabbeinu Barukh and Rabbeinu Shimon of Sens disagreed about this at length, whether there are lashes for unwitting substitution, and they found divergent books here; and I explained it at the beginning of our tractate. However, shortly below, in the case of one who thinks that sacrificial animals that developed a blemish are eaten without redemption, we cannot read “with regard to sacrificial animals it is not consecrated,” since it was already consecrated from the outset. Rather, this is how we read there: “With regard to substitution he is flogged; with regard to sacrificial animals he is not flogged.”
tosafot:a9.1: “I will enter this house, etc.,” and he consecrated without his awareness: Rashi explained that he was a man lost in his thoughts and did not know what he was saying. And this is difficult: why does he need to say “I will enter this house,” etc.? Therefore it seems right to explain “I will enter this house,” etc., as meaning: When I enter this house, this animal shall at once be a substitute and that one shall be consecrated, with my awareness. And he entered it, and substituted and consecrated without his awareness, for he said nothing upon entering and also did not think about what he had said at first; it turns out that the substitution and the consecration took effect without his awareness.
tosafot:a13.1: If so, a tereifa too is sacrificed in its kind: But he does not raise a difficulty from the others, for a tumtum and a hermaphrodite are anomalous creatures, and it is as though their kind is not sacrificed. And so too, at an animal born by caesarean section people are astonished, and it is as though its kind is not sacrificed. And so too, diverse kinds are anomalous, and it is as though their kind is not sacrificed. And so Rashi explained.
gershom:a1.1: He rendered unwitting like intentional with regard to substitution, but not with regard to sacrificial animals.
gershom:a2.1: With regard to substitution he is flogged: for it is written “shall be holy,” to include unwitting like intentional.
gershom:a3.1: And with regard to sacrificial animals he is not flogged: if he acted unwittingly. But one who consecrates an animal with a permanent blemish intentionally transgresses five prohibitions, as we said in the first chapter.
gershom:a4.1: He thought: to consecrate a red one, and he consecrated a black one [the Davidson English reads black and white]. It is not consecrated, as we learned: consecration in error, Beit Shammai say it is consecration and Beit Hillel say it is not consecration.
gershom:a5.1: Such as where he said: Let this one go out to non-sacred status and let that one enter as a substitute in its sanctity. With regard to substitution he is flogged, as we said in the first chapter: “He shall not exchange it,” with others’ animals that are not his; that is: let mine go out to non-sacred status and be so-and-so’s, and that one of his shall be its substitute. It is consecrated and he is flogged, for it is substitution.
gershom:a6.1: With regard to sacrificial animals: he is not flogged, for “shall be” is not written about them.
gershom:a7.1: It is taught: Rabbi Meir said: Since, etc., as we explained in the first chapter. You find it only in the offspring of sacrificial animals, which are consecrated by virtue of their mothers, and in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who said that with other offspring of sacrificial animals the offspring effects substitution. But these do not sanctify to effect substitution, for their sanctity is not strong.
gershom:a8.1: He holds that their law is like that of a non-kosher animal.
gershom:a9.1: But there is a blemished animal, which is not sacrificed, and yet it is consecrated with inherent sanctity, as it teaches that substitution takes effect on it, and substitution is inherent sanctity.
gershom:a10.1: A blemished animal has its kind that is sacrificed; therefore it is consecrated with inherent sanctity.
gershom:a11.1: So too any inherent disqualification, such as these, diverse kinds and a tereifa: they are not consecrated with inherent sanctity. To exclude a blemished animal, which is a disqualification of a lacking limb and is consecrated with inherent sanctity.
gershom:a12.1: But isn’t “too long” and “closed” written in the passage of blemished animals, and these have nothing lacking: for “too long” [sarua] is one whose thigh is extended, and “closed” [kalut] is one whose hooves are closed like those of a donkey. These are not disqualifications of something lacking but inherent disqualifications, like a tereifa, and yet they are consecrated with inherent sanctity, as with a substitute.
gershom:a13.1: To exclude a blemished animal, which has its kind that is sacrificed [unlike one that has no kind that is sacrificed]. And if it is difficult for you: a tereifa too has its kind that is sacrificed, and it is similar to a blemished animal, whose kind is sacrificed, so let it be consecrated with inherent sanctity like a blemished animal:
gershom:a14.1: It is not similar: a tereifa to a blemished animal in this matter that we want to say. Rather, it is similar to a non-kosher animal: just as a non-kosher animal is forbidden for consumption, so too a tereifa is forbidden for consumption, and it is not consecrated with inherent sanctity, like a non-kosher animal. To exclude a blemished animal, which is permitted for consumption; therefore it is consecrated with inherent sanctity.
gershom:a15.1: It requires a permanent blemish to be redeemed on its account: if he wishes to redeem it.
gershom:a16.1: Conclude from it that one redeems sacrificial animals to feed them to dogs: for it is not fit for human consumption, since it is a tereifa, and is fit only for dogs. Rather, it becomes sanctified to die: it is not subject to redemption; rather, one puts it into a chamber and it dies of itself. That is to say, inherent sanctity takes effect on it.
gershom:a17.1: And this disagrees with Rabbi Oshaya, who said: one who consecrates a tereifa is like one who dedicates wood and stones alone; that is to say, it is sanctity of value. The reason [the mishna rules that one may not redeem them] is that he consecrated it and afterward it became a tereifa.
gershom:a18.1: You find: that it is consecrated with inherent sanctity.
gershom:a19.1: But if it was a tereifa from the outset: before he consecrated it, it is not consecrated with inherent sanctity.
gershom:a20.1: He holds: this tanna, Rabbi Elazar, holds that whatever is not fit for sacrifice is not consecrated with inherent sanctity. Conclude from it that he holds it is not consecrated with inherent sanctity, and this is a refutation of Shmuel, who said “it becomes sanctified to die,” which is inherent sanctity. [On the mishna:] he holds that even though it is not fit for sacrifice, if they were tereifa from the outset, before he consecrated them, one may redeem them; evidently it is not consecrated with inherent sanctity. Teach [instead]: if they were tereifa from the outset, one may not redeem them.
gershom:a21.1: Or if you wish, say: it actually teaches “that became,” and one infers from it that if they were tereifa [from the outset] one may redeem them; this tanna holds that anywhere, etc.
gershom:a22.1: We will return to you, Yesh BaKorbanot.
rashi:b1.1: Shmuel can say to you: Rabbi Eliezer [the daf reads Rabbi Elazar] holds that anywhere it is not fit, etc., and I, who said [my ruling], hold in accordance with the Rabbis.
rashi:b1.2: Perhaps: whose view is this, which teaches “but if they were so from the outset, one may redeem them”? It is Rabbi Eliezer’s [the daf reads Rabbi Elazar].
rashi:b3.1: These: [the heading of Rashi’s note on the new mishna; no comment follows it.]
rashi:b4.1: And since it taught “their offspring and the offspring of their offspring”: why do I need it to teach “until the end of the world”?
rashi:b4.2: He heard Rabbi Eliezer [the daf reads Rabbi Elazar], who said: in the mishna, the offspring of a peace offering is not sacrificed, but rather is left to die.
rashi:b5.1: “Male”: concerning peace offerings, as it is stated: “And if his offering be a sacrifice of peace offerings,” etc. The verse should have written: “If he offer of the herd, he shall offer it without blemish.” Why do I need “if male, if female,” if not for exposition?
rashi:b6.1: Is sacrificed: as is included shortly from “female.”
rashi:b7.1: In all sacrificial animals: offerings of an individual.
rashi:b7.2: The offspring does not apply in all sacrificial animals: for a burnt offering and a guilt offering are males.
rashi:b8.1: And the offspring of unblemished animals: whose mother is unblemished.
rashi:b9.1: And I will reverse: “if male” to include the substitute of blemished animals, and “if female” to include the offspring of blemished animals.
rashi:b9.2: From the place where it was included: the substitute of unblemished animals was included from “female”; therefore the substitute of blemished animals was included from the “if” adjacent to it, and not from the “if” adjacent to “male.”
rashi:b10.1: The whole verse: “male” to include the substitute, and its “if” for the substitute of blemished animals; “female” to include the offspring, and its “if” for the offspring of blemished animals.
rashi:b10.2: Indicates a masculine form: therefore it is derived from “male.”
rashi:b11.1: For what halakha: are these offspring of blemished animals consecrated? For their mother is not fit to be sacrificed.
rashi:b11.2: And according to Rabbi Elazar: who said in the mishna: If one set aside a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth, its offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering, even though its mother is not fit. Here too, they are sacrificed even though their mother is not fit, and it was necessary to teach us this.
rashi:b12.1: Lest you say: it is there that Rabbi Elazar said so, with regard to a burnt offering, since the name of burnt offering applies to its mother; that is to say, even though she herself is not sacrificed, sanctity does not depart from her, for we find a female burnt offering, such as a bird burnt offering, since unblemished status and maleness are not required in birds.
rashi:b12.2: But with regard to the offspring: of blemished peace offerings, where the name of peace offering does not apply to their mother, for we do not find a blemished animal sacrificed as a peace offering, since there is no peace offering of birds, I would say that they are not sacrificed.
rashi:b13.1: According to all: for even the Rabbis concede that they are at least consecrated for grazing, and we do not say that they are non-sacred, since we also say with regard to a female burnt offering that its offspring shall graze.
rashi:b16.1: One might have thought that one should bring it into the Temple and withhold from them, etc.: for then “you shall take and go” has been fulfilled.
rashi:b16.2: “And you shall offer your burnt offerings … and the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out,” etc. (Deuteronomy 12:27): and this verse is adjacent to “only your holy things.”
rashi:b17.1: One might have thought that all sacrificial animals too: that their offspring and their substitute are also sacrificed.
rashi:b17.2: The verse states “only”: and below it explains which offspring it excludes. All occurrences of “akh” and “rak” are restrictions.
rashi:b19.1: From where would it come: that it would enter your mind that they should die, so that “your burnt offerings,” etc., was needed? Certainly, since we learn that five sin offerings die, two of them being the offspring of a sin offering and the substitute of a sin offering, by implication the offspring of a peace offering and the substitute of a peace offering do not come to that, for it was learned only with regard to a sin offering.
tosafot:b4.1: It is not necessary to say with regard to the offspring that I do not concede to you; rather, even until the end of the world I do not concede to you: And if you say: let it teach “until the end of the world” and not teach “their offspring and the offspring of their offspring”? One can say that it teaches “not only this but also this,” for that is the way of the Mishna, to teach in this manner. And it is puzzling, for at the beginning of HaKotev (Ketubot 83b) the Gemara asks whether “produce of the produce” is precise, or “until the end of the world” is precise, or both are precise, and here it does not ask so. One can say that there they are exacting about wording written in a document, since one should not write in a document something that is unnecessary, but in the wording of the Mishna there is no need to be so exacting. And at the beginning of tractate Yevamot (2a) the Gemara is not exacting, as it is here, to ask: since it taught “their rival wives and the rival wives of their rival wives,” why do I need “until the end of the world”? For it is obvious to it that all of them needed to be taught, since we would not have known that rival wives and the rival wives of rival wives are exempt had it not taught all of them.
tosafot:b7.1: “Female” to include the substitute: And even though it is written (Leviticus 27:10): “Then both it and that for which it is changed shall be holy,” a verse was needed to include that it is sacrificed. And if you say: what is different, that here a verse was needed to include that it is sacrificed, while with regard to the firstborn and the tithe “they” is written, from which we exclude: [they,] and not their offspring nor their substitute? One can say: since a restriction is written with regard to the firstborn and the tithe, a verse was needed here to include.
tosafot:b12.1: Since the name of burnt offering applies to its mother: Rashi explained: that is to say, a female belongs to [the category of] burnt offering, for we find a female burnt offering in the bird burnt offering, since unblemished status and maleness are not required in birds; but with regard to the offspring of blemished peace offerings, the name of sacrificial animals does not apply to their mother, for we do not find a blemished animal sacrificed as a peace offering, since there is no peace offering of birds. End of his words. [On this reading:] “Bar Padda said: for grazing, and according to all,” for even Rabbi Eliezer, who said that one who sets aside a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth, the offspring itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering, his reason is that the name of burnt offering applies to its mother, meaning in a bird burnt offering. And this is difficult for Rashi’s explanation: for if so, that the name of bird burnt offering that applies to the mother is effective for the offspring, then if one set aside a blemished female for a burnt offering and it gave birth, we should say that the offspring itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering, since the name of bird burnt offering applies to its mother; yet it implies that it excludes every offspring of blemished animals. Furthermore, below it implies that the mother’s [status as a] bird burnt offering is not effective for the offspring. And it seems right to my teacher, the Rav M. R. [abbreviated in the text], to explain “the name of burnt offering applies to its mother” as meaning that she is consecrated with inherent sanctity when one set aside a female and it gave birth, for she has no redemption; therefore it is right that the offspring itself be sacrificed. But blemished animals, on which there is no inherent sanctity at all, it is not right that their offspring be sacrificed; rather, they should graze. [So] my teacher, the Rav M. R.
tosafot:b21.1: If of a burnt offering, it is male: and is not capable of giving birth; and as for its substitute, it is certainly sacrificed. And if of a guilt offering, it is learned as a halakha that it goes to grazing. The same holds that it could have said “it is male and not capable of giving birth,” as with a burnt offering, but it preferred to raise the difficulty from another matter. And if you say: according to Rabbeinu Tam, who said that it is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai that wherever with a sin offering the animal dies, with a guilt offering it is sacrificed as a burnt offering, why does it not establish [the baraita] as referring to a guilt offering? One can say that it could not establish it so, since it is obvious to it that it is not sacrificed as a guilt offering, and “only” implies that it excludes it from being sacrificed as the kind of offering it comes from; therefore it was not needed, for it is obvious that it is not sacrificed as a guilt offering.
gershom:b1.1: These are sacrificial animals whose offspring and substitutes are like them: they are sacrificed. The offspring of peace offerings and their substitute, and the offspring of the offspring of peace offerings, until the end of all the world: their law is like peace offerings. We heard that Rabbi Elazar said: the offspring of a peace offering is not sacrificed as a peace offering, but rather grazes.
gershom:b2.1: It is not necessary [to say] that their offspring is sacrificed as a peace offering, etc.
gershom:b3.1: “If male”: this is the verse that is written: “And if his offering be a sacrifice of peace offerings: if he offer of the herd, if male, if female.” For “if male, if female” was not needed, since it said “of the herd” without qualification, which implies both male and female. Rather, it was needed for this: “male” to include the offspring and “female” to include the substitute.
gershom:b4.1: Let it write “female,” and it would not need to write “male” for the sake of the offspring, for one could derive the offspring from the substitute by an a fortiori inference.
gershom:b5.1: “But could this not be derived,” etc.: and let us derive the substitute from the offspring, and a verse would not be needed: “But could this not be derived,” etc. [Rabbeinu Gershom also runs the inference the other way, from offspring to substitute.]
gershom:b6.1: “What about the offspring, which is grown from consecrated property; shall you say,” etc.: for this reason it was necessary to write both, “male” and “female.”
gershom:b7.1: From where do we derive that the offspring of blemished animals and the substitute of blemished animals are sacrificed: a blemished animal whose consecration preceded its blemish, which effects substitution, as we say: what was good from the outset effects substitution.
gershom:b8.1: When it says “if”: from “if,” “if,” they are included.
gershom:b9.1: To be sacrificed, and according to Rabbi Elazar, who said in the mishna: One who sets aside a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth to a male, the offspring shall graze until it becomes blemished, and so too the mother, since it is not right to bring a female burnt offering; Rabbi Elazar says: the offspring itself shall be sacrificed as a burnt offering. For lest you say: when Rabbi Elazar said that the offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering, that is where the name of burnt offering applies to its mother, for we find a female burnt offering among birds, in the bird burnt offering, as we say that unblemished status and maleness are not required in birds, so one may bring a female bird burnt offering; but these offspring and substitutes of blemished animals, where the name of peace offering does not apply to blemished animals, say that Rabbi Elazar holds they are not sacrificed. It teaches us that Rabbi Elazar too holds that they are sacrificed, like the offspring of a burnt offering. And the Rabbis disagree with him, [holding] that they graze. [A printer’s note here suggests reading: “It teaches us that even with the substitute of blemished animals Rabbi Elazar holds that they are sacrificed.”]
gershom:b10.1: Bar Padda said: say that it includes them not to be sacrificed but only for grazing, and it accords with all opinions, both the Rabbis and Rabbi Elazar; for Rabbi Elazar said only with regard to the offspring of a burnt offering that it is sacrificed, since the name of burnt offering applies to its mother, but not these. Say the reverse: that from the “if” of “male” the substitutes of blemished animals are included, and from the “if” of “female” the offspring of blemished animals are included. He said to him: it stands to reason that from where the offspring of unblemished animals is included, from “male,” from there, from its “if,” the offspring of blemished animals are included; and from where the substitute of an unblemished animal is included, from “female,” from its “if” the substitutes of blemished animals are included. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s order places this exchange after bar Padda’s statement.]
gershom:b11.1: Rav Pappa [the daf reads Rav Safra] said to him: Did I say to you to reverse “if,” “if”? I am speaking of reversing the whole verse, and this is what I say: “if male” to include the substitute, and its “if” to include blemished animals; and “female” to include the offspring, and its “if” to include the offspring of blemished animals. He said to him: you cannot say so, for “offspring” implies a masculine form, so it is included from “male,” and “substitute” implies a feminine form, so it is included from “if female.” And this tanna brings it, for the offspring and for the substitutes, from this verse:
gershom:b12.1: “Only your holy things”: these are the substitutes, for a substitute too is called holy.
gershom:b13.1: “That you have” implies: these are the offspring, which will be born from the sacrificial animals. For since the verse says “you shall take and go” to the place and nothing more, I would understand that once he has brought them there he need not do more, but may bring them into the Temple and withhold water and food from them so that they die, and be exempt.
gershom:b14.1: The verse states, adjacent to it: “And you shall offer your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood”: in the manner that you treat a burnt offering, to sprinkle its blood and burn it entirely, so you treat its substitute; and in the manner that you treat peace offerings, so you treat their offspring and their substitute: placing hands, libations and the waving of the breast and thigh, as it is written: “And the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out … and you shall eat the flesh.” One might have thought that the offspring of all sacrificial animals too would have the law of their mothers.
gershom:b15.1: The verse states “only”: it excluded the offspring of other sacrificial animals.
gershom:b16.1: Rabbi Akiva says: it is not necessary to learn from “only” to exclude the offspring and substitutes of other sacrificial animals; you can derive it from here:
gershom:b17.1: “It is a guilt offering”: it itself is sacrificed, but not its substitute, and so too the substitute of other sacrificial animals. [On the Gemara that follows:] From where would this come, that he would be permitted to withhold food from them so that they die? But since we learned, etc. Which offspring could you say, of the other sacrificial animals, is sacrificed?
